subject: Coffee & Tea
title: How Britain Fell in Love With Tea
description: A fast breakdown of How Britain Fell in Love With Tea for builders.

hook.text: Britain drinks 100 million cups of tea every day—more per capita than almost anywhere except Turkey and Ireland.

buildup.text: Tea arrived in England in the 1660s when Catherine of Braganza—a Portuguese princess—married Charles II.

discovery.text: Catherine brought her tea-drinking habit to court. The aristocracy copied the queen, and tea became fashionable overnight.

twist.text: Tea was initially so expensive that families kept it in locked wooden chests—the original 'tea caddies.'

climax.text: As prices dropped in the 1800s, tea went from luxury to necessity. Even factory workers got tea breaks.

punchline.text: A queen's habit became a nation's identity. Britain runs on tea.

quiz.question: Who popularized tea in the English court?
options: Catherine of Braganza, wife of Charles II

details.summary: Britain's transformation from a coffee-drinking nation to the world's most devoted tea culture happened over the 1700s. Cheap imports from the East India Company, sugar from Caribbean plantations, and royal endorsement combined to make tea Britain's national drink.
details.whyItMatters: Britain's tea love story shows how trade, colonialism, and cultural fashion can permanently reshape a nation's identity. It was not inevitable but the product of specific historical forces.
takeaways: Britain shifted from coffee to tea over the 1700s
East India Company imports made tea affordable for all classes
Sugar and milk made tea palatable across social groups

faq.question: Was Britain always a tea-drinking nation?
faq.answer: No. In the 1600s, London had thousands of coffeehouses and coffee was the fashionable drink. Tea became dominant only in the 1700s as the East India Company made it more affordable and marketing targeted domestic consumption. The shift was driven by economics more than taste.

faq.question: How much tea do the British drink today?
faq.answer: About 100 million cups per day, or roughly 36 billion cups per year. Per capita consumption is around 1.9 kilograms annually, making Britain one of the top tea-consuming nations. The habit is declining slightly among younger generations but remains deeply embedded in daily life.
